Ministers—Confidence
1. Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE (Lea der of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister:
Does he have confidence that his Ministers are ethical and competent?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Can he assure the public that  the Hon Nick Smith, the Hon
Peter Dunne, and the Hon John Banks all upheld to his satisfaction the requirements of
the Cabinet Manual that “… Ministers are expected to  act lawfully and to behave in a
way that upholds, and is seen to uphold, the highest ethical standards.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: This is going to come as a gr eat revelation to the member, but
John Banks is no longer a Minister.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: In light of that answer and given that John Banks has
conveniently forgotten helicopter rides, 7-foot-tall German billionaires, and the
concurrent arrival of two cheques for $25,000, how  is it credible for the Prime Minister
to even consider reappointing him to a mi nisterial role as he  said he would do
yesterday?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: It strikes me that the member keeps forgetting what he tells
private audiences he is in. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have a point of order.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speak er. I appreciate that the question
had an introductory part to it, but the Pr ime Minister should make some attempt to
address it.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I think that question would fa ll into the category that you
often mention and that your predecessors in that seat often mentioned: very heavily
loaded political questions. What the Prime Minist er did was refer to the first part of that
question and I think adequately addressed it.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: On this occasion I am going to accept the advice given by the Hon
Gerry Brownlee. The question was very pol itically loaded. When members ask a
supplementary question like that, they give a fair amount of licen ce to a Minister or
Prime Minister to answer.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Given that the Prime Minister said yesterday that he would
reinstate John Banks but would only possibly reinstate the Hon Peter Dunne, can he tell
the House why his confidence in the Hon Pete r Dunne is lower than in the Hon John
Banks?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I have no ministerial responsibility for that.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The Prime Minister does
have responsibility for statements that he  made, and he was being asked to reconcile
two of those statements. That is a perfectly acceptable question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: On this occasion I accept the advice of the member Grant
Robertson. I am going to ask the Hon David Cunliffe to re-ask that question.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Given that he said yesterday that he would reinstate John
Banks but would only possibly reinstate the Hon Peter Dunne , can he tell the House
why his confidence in the Hon Peter Dunne is lower?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: It is not.
14178 Questions for Oral Answer 23 Oct 2013

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Does he believe that Nick Smith simply forgot about being
briefed on the Ruataniwha dam before 29 July the first eight times he was asked about it
in the House, even though the dam submission had been mentioned three times
previously in the Minister’s weekly reports?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Mr Speaker, I understand that you are yet to make a ruling on
the privileges complaint in relation to this matter, and I do not believe that it is
appropriate to discuss the matter until you have done so.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Does he think it is appropriate for the Minister of Conservation
to interfere in a departmental decision and to stop the department from raising
legitimate concerns about water quality to the Ruataniwha dam board of inquiry?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I think that Doris Johnston made it quite clear that the
Minister did not.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I delayed raising this
point of order because I thought it would be obvious to you that when Mr Key said that
a matter was brought before you for a privil eges decision, he acted as though you were
some fine judicial court and the matter was sub judice. It wi ll be very ap parent to you
that you are not and the issue is not, so he should not have been able to get away with
that.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I am not sure exactly what the point of order is. Maybe the Hon
Gerry Brownlee could help. [ Interruption] Order! This is a point of order. It will be
heard in silence.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: It was perfectly reasonable in the answer for the Prime
Minister to acknowledge the le tter to you from the Hon Davi d Cunliffe, relating to the
matter of privilege, and s uggesting that it would be inappropriate to make any
prejudicial comments when it is in your hands. I think that is perfectly acceptable.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I accept that. I agree entirely.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Given this sorry litany of ministerial failures, and the fact that
his ragtag Government is hanging by a th read, is his plan C to inflate crazy,
conservative Colin Craig, or is he just a “Mad Hatter” looking for a new tea party?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am sorry that the member cannot count, but we actually have
64 votes, so we are not hanging by a thread. If he wants to get into crazy, he could look
at his own coalition partners. Bu t, actually, he does not have to look too far. He should
just follow the advice of Trevor Mallard, who nicely summed up last night exactly what
he thought of Metiria Turei.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: How can the Prime Minister be  contemplating restoring to
a ministerial post someone who leaked from  the Government Communications Security
Bureau (GCSB) four separate times, and a fi fth time, which was in respect of the Inland
Revenue Department and Novopay; how can that person possibly be—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: Tell us about the gnome.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: The difference is that I did not lie to the House like you
did.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is a very good example of the unhelpful information of
an interjection, but then the re sponse from the Rt Hon Winst on Peters was out of order.
Would the member now rise to his feet and simply ask his supplementary question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I would be very grateful to. How can the Prime Minister be
possibly contemplating restoring to a Cabinet post someone who leaked information in
respect of the GCSB four se parate times, and a fifth time in respect of the Inland
Revenue Department and Novopay; how can th at person possibly fit the high standards
that he has hitherto claimed to uphold?
23 Oct 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14179

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Firstly, the premise of the que stion is wrong. It is unproven in
terms of the first point, and the second point is  that if he wants to talk reinstatement,
maybe he should talk to Brendan Horan. I understand he might have been—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is not helpful to the order of the House.
Economic Growth—Forecasts and Reports
2. DAVID BENNETT (National—Hamilton East)  to the Minister of Finance :
What reports has he received on building momentum in the New Zealand economy and
how this is supporting jobs?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yesterday the ASB released its
quarterly economic forecast pointing to a broad-based improvement in business activity.
This follows encouraging reports from other forecasters. The higher dairy payout will
add $4 billion of income to the regional econo my, and that sits alongside a recovery in
meat prices, although livestock numbers will take some time to rebuild from the
drought. The Canterbury rebuild is gain ing traction, and ASB says the Auckland
housing market is on the cusp of a housi ng construction pick-up. Recent migration
figures show fewer New Zealanders are leav ing for Australia because of the relative
improvement in the New Zealand labour market, meaning they are relatively more
likely to get a job here than they are in Au stralia. This is an encouraging picture of
consistent economic growth.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: How is the improved economic momentum being reflected in
business and consumer confidence, and what growth does this point to over the next few
years?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Last week the ANZ released its survey of consumer
confidence. Confidence was up in September and remains above the long-term levels of
consumer confidence. Consumers report feelin g better off than a year ago, and more
likely to buy a major household item. ANZ al so reports that business sentiment is
strong. These confidence levels point to reasonably good economic growth in the year
ahead, with higher incomes and more jobs for more New Zealanders.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: How is increasing confidence among businesses and consumers
delivering jobs and growth in the economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It is important th at there are new jobs in the economy,
because in any given quarter up to 100,000 jobs disappear from the economy.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: What about the regions?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: So it is pleasing to see higher levels of confidence
translating into rising employ ment. TradeMe jobs reports that  job listings are up nearly
10 percent from what they were a year ago. Manawat ū and Wanganui job listings are up
17 percent, and they are regions. Bay of Pl enty listings are up 13 percent, and I
understand that the Bay of Plenty is regard ed as a region. The SEEK website reports
that the strongest growth in  job listings is in the S outh Island, in particular
Marlborough, which is a region, the West Co ast, which is certainly a region, and
Southland, which is somewhat metropolitan but probably a region.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What reports has the Minister received endorsing the Government’s
economic programme and the current improvement in the New Zealand economic
direction?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: There are so many of these reports, but some of them are
particularly satisfying. There was one last night, and I will quote it, in respect of the
economy: “It’s certainly heading in the right dire ction. We celebrate the improvement.”
That actually was on Television New Zeala nd yesterday morning, from the current
leader of the Labour Party, David Cunliffe.
14180 Questions for Oral Answer 23 Oct 2013

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: What steps to prevent the recent closure of a Shannon
fellmongery and a Rotorua sawmill, with larg e job losses, did the Government take,
including addressing a grossly overvalued exchange rate, now heading towards US90c?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: We share the member’s concern about the value of the
exchange rate. The single most important m easure the Government is taking to do what
it can to relieve pressure on the exchange rate  is to increase the supply of housing more
quickly on the ground, particularly in Auckland.  The Minister of Housing, just a couple
of weeks ago, announced special housing areas for 5,000 houses. Otherwise, our
exchange rate is determined  largely by the state of the US economy. As it continues to
improve it is likely that our exchange rate will be re-rated downwards.
Skycity, Convention Centre—Members’ Potential Conflicts of Interest
3. METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green) to the Prime Minister: Has he checked
his files yet regarding whethe r Hon John Banks declared a po tential conflict of interest
in relation to the New Zeal and International Convention Centre Bill while still a
Minister; if so, was any conflict declared?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, and no.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Prime Minister consider that John Banks, while a Minister
is his Government, acted in strict accordance with the Cabinet Manual regarding the
declaration of conflict of inte rest, given that no such conflic t of interest concerning the
Skycity bill was declared by John Banks?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, and I do not believe that there was a conflict.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Prime Minister not agree that a Minister who is the subject
of court evidence given by someone involved in a multimillion-dollar deal that requires
that Minister’s vote in the House to pass ha s a conflict of interest; if so, does that
conflict of interest remain once that person is no longer a Minister?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, I do not believe there was a conflict of interest, any more
than there would be a conflict of interest—if we want to follow the member’s logic—
where Labour would be voting on employment  legislation when we know that the
unions actually have a vote in the Labour membership. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have called Metiria Turei for a supplementary question.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Did the Prime Minister discuss any potential conflict of interest in
relation to the New Zealand In ternational Convention Centre  Bill with Skycity Chief
Executive Nigel Morrison when he was hanging  out with him at the opening of the new
Skycity bar in Auckland last week?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, and I am pleased that the member looked at the Herald on
Sunday, where I was photographed at that particular opening with many other people.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Is the Prime Minister concerned by reports of yet anot her conflict of
interest concerning the bill, where Na tional MP and Commerce Committee member
Sam Lotu-Iiga sat silently by while his electorate chair misinformed the select
committee about the Catholic Church’s position on the Skycity bill; if not—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The question is addressed to  the Prime Minister, who has no
responsibility either for what occurred at a select committee or for a member of the
caucus. It is a question the member is asking of the Prime Minister as a Minister. I will
give the opportunity for the member to rephrase that question.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Has the Prime Minister seen the reports, and is he concerned by the
reports, of yet another conflict of intere st concerning a Nationa l MP who sat on the
Commerce Committee silently while his electorate secretary gave misinformation to the
committee about the Catholic Church’s pos ition on the Skycity bill; if he is not
concerned, why not?
23 Oct 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14181

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I believe that what the
member has just asked is essentially the sa me question that you have  just ruled on. It
gets to the point where we would have to, for example, have members of the Labour
Party recusing themselves from select comm ittees if one of the unions was appearing,
or, if Greenpeace was appearing, the Green Party would have to leave the select
committee. Members are expected to exercise  a degree of discretion in these matters. I
do not think that there has been anything wrong with this, and the qu estion, in itself, is
out of order.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I would just remind the member, and I also say this for your
consideration, Mr Speaker, that my questio n concerned whether the Prime Minister had
seen any reports or had any concern about any such reports. He does have responsibility
for that.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The difficulty that the member has, and she has tried to abide by the
Standing Orders, is that the Prime Minister does not have responsibility. The member is
not going to make the grade in asking the que stion by trying to rephrase it. I will not
rule the question out; I will give the me mber effectively anot her shot at another
question.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Thank you very much, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Very generous. [Interruption] Order!

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Has the Prime Minister had any di scussions with Cabinet regarding
the Catholic Church’s position being misrepresented by Sam Lotu-Iiga’s electorate
chairperson while Sam Lotu-Iiga was on that committee; if so, did any member of his
Cabinet express any concerns regarding the mi srepresentation of the Catholic Church’s
position?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Rt Hon Prime Minister, as far as he has a responsibility.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, I have not had any discussions with Cabinet. In relation to
reports, yes, I have seen one report, which came from Trevor Mallard. It said that the
member is not on top of her job, and I agree with Trevor Mallard. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. If that last comment
from the Prime Minister could in any way be  construed as being in, and related to, the
question, then every part of the member’s primary and supplementary questions should
have been allowed in, by the licence you gave the Prime Minister.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member raises qu ite a valid point on this  occasion. The answer
from the Prime Minister was not helpful to th e order of the House, but at the end of the
day he was actually responding to an interjec tion that came from the Opposition side of
the House.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Will the Prime Minister require all members of his Cabinet or his
Government to declare any personal or financia l conflict of interest that they may have
in voting for the Skycity bill and make those declarations public?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Cabinet Ministers already follow rules in relation to conflicts
of interest. They work with the Cabinet Office  to ensure that they follow the rules, and
in my experience of seeing them in action, they follow those rules closely.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Has the Prime Minister discusse d with his Cabinet any concerns
about the fact that the New Zealand Inte rnational Convention Centre Bill may get
through only because of votes from John Ba nks, who has an undeclared conflict of
interest, and Sam Lotu-Iiga, who kept silent  over his electorate chair misrepresenting
the views of the Catholic Church to the Commerce Committee?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If the right honourable Prime Minister could answer the first part of
that question.
14182 Questions for Oral Answer 23 Oct 2013

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, I think the member is wr ong. In fact, I think the member
is out to lunch.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, it is not in order for the Prime Minister to answer that last part
of the answer in that way. Would he stand, withdraw, and apologise for that.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I withdraw and apologise.
District Health Boards—Health Benefits Ltd
4. Hon ANNETTE KING (Labour—Rongotai)  to the Minister of Health : Is he
satisfied with the performance of Health Benefits Ltd; if so, why?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Yes, within the challenge of
standardising administrative and procurement processes across 20 district health boards,
which have generally been operating independe ntly. The goal of this 5-year strategy is
to use the power of standardisation in bulk purchasing to move resources from the back
office to the front line. This is very impor tant, because back-office administration staff
numbers grew by over 40 percent, or from  8,000 to close to 12,000, under the previous
Labour Government.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: What concerns does he have about the ability of Health Benefits
Ltd to actually achieve the $700 million in cuts to district health boards over the next 2
years, in light of the fact that the Health Committee was told by Health Benefits Ltd that
no breakdown of the cuts was available?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I am very confident that it is going to be able to meet the
achievements set out in its State-owned enterp rise statement of intent. I would have to
say that the member is quite wrong to characterise these as cuts, because they are
actually savings from procurement activitie s. So, for example, moving to one bank
nationally, bringing the distri ct health boards’ overnight bank accounts together, has
saved $4 million, which goes straight back into  front-line services for patients. That is
not a cut; that is a saving.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Has he seen a breakdown of the cuts claimed to have been made
by Health Benefits Ltd, such as  in this report leaked to me a few days ago; if he has
seen such information, can he give an assu rance that the $2 million that has been cut
from wound care is not affecting the recovery of patients?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I cannot see that schedule from here, but what I can tell the
member is that Health Benefits Ltd is making a significant c ontribution in making
savings. So, for example, moving from havi ng 18 suppliers of gloves to six has saved
$6 million over a 3-year period. Similarly, through better negotiations of insurance
arrangements, Health Benefits Ltd has contributed to savings of almost $7 million in the
insurance costs for district health boards.  When you have inherited a situation where
bureaucracy—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That answer is now getting quite long enough.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I seek leave to table the leaked report I have of a ll the cuts that
have been made because—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is enough of a descri ption. It was described well in the
supplementary question. Leave is sought to tabl e that particular document. Is there any
objection? There is objection.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Why was this information deni ed to the select committee and
what is there to hide, or is there concern already that the $1.1 million that has been cut
from children’s oral health is adversely affecting their dental care?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I would have to check the veracity of the member’s
information, because my—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. I sought leave to table the
very—
23 Oct 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14183

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! I want to know what the point of order
is.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: My point of order is that the Minister is chal lenging my word,
based on something—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The Minister had said he would have to seek validation of
your words, or words to that effect.

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I know that over the last 4 months the member has submitted
over 400 Official Information Act requests to di strict health boards, so I am unable to
comment on every single one of them. But what I can say—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Sorry, but my question was
not about how many Official Information Act requests I have sent to district health
boards. I asked why this information was not available to the select committee.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The difficulty we have now got is  that I can hardly remember the
question because I have had two points of order.  So what we will do to try to tidy it up
is we will get the member to ask the question again, and we will get the Minister to
attempt to answer it.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Why was this information deni ed to the select committee and
what is there to hide, or is there c oncern that the $1.1 million already cut from
children’s oral health is adversely affecting their dental care?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I think there has been a remarkable amount of information put
out about Health Benefits Ltd. I would have to check the detail of what that member has
said. It may be like her response to the South Canterbury Dist rict Health Board’s
numbers, where, in an Official Informati on Act request, the figures were amended. The
member has not yet explained why she did that. But what I do know is that Health
Benefits Ltd is making considerable savings th at are being delivered to patient care. For
example—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. The Minister has strayed a
long way from the original question, and I think it is probably time to move to the next
question, do you not?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! On this occasion, the me mber is not correct. The Hon
Annette King asked three questions. The first was why the information was denied to
the select committee. The second question was wh at there is to hide. That is the one the
Minister is spending some time answering. The third question was then something about
oral health. Members risk getting a confused an swer that will not be to their satisfaction
when they ask a supplementary question that actually has three parts to it.

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: What Health Benefits Ltd is doing is it is making savings in
administrative and procurement costs that are being used to improve oral health and
other services. I can tell that member that th e number of kids who are waiting to see a
dental therapist is far lower than when I became Minister of Health.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Has he been advised that Health Benefits Ltd’s finance supply
chain and procurement project has had little planning, is ca using considerable concern,
and is resulting in increased costs to distri ct health boards; if so, what action has he
taken to stop a potential disaster?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Of course district health boards are going to invest some
money to make quite considerable savings in  the future. For example, with the changes
that we are making to finance procurem ent and supply chain management, it is
estimated that we are going to save consid erable hundreds of milli ons of dollars over a
10-year period. All that money is going to go back into front-line services for patients—
more elective surgery, faster cancer treatment , better access to emergency departments.
We simply cannot carry on as Labour did, with a 40 percent—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That answer is now quite long enough.

Christchurch, Recovery—Central Business District Anchor Projects
5. NICKY WAGNER (National—Christchurch Central)  to the Minister for

items.speaker: Canterbury Earthquake Recovery
items.text: What recent progress has been made on the
anchor projects in the Christchurch Central recovery plan?
Very good progress is being made. Last week  the Prime Minister unveiled the design
for the $300 million Christchurch Justice and Emergency Services Precinct. Earthworks
are scheduled to begin in the next 4 months , making this the first major public building
built in Christchurch since the earthquake s. Other anchor projects are gathering
momentum, including the bus interchange, with  construction due to begin in the early
part of next year; the hospita l redevelopment, which is under way, or, at least, planning
is well down the track; and that leads us to  the convention centre, for which significant
expressions of interest are currently being considered.

items.speaker: Nicky Wagner
items.text: How are the anchor projects pr oviding examples of better public
services?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: The rebuild provides an opportunity for innovations
and the capturing of efficiencies in the way publ ic service is offered, rather than simply
doing things the way they were done before. The justice precinct is a premier example
of this, and leads strongly to a better public service. It will house several justice sector
agencies in one location, enabling them to share facilities and services and work
together more effectively. This will be the largest multi-agency Government project in
New Zealand’s history.

items.speaker: Nicky Wagner
items.text: Why are the anchor projects important  to the recovery of the central
city?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: The anchor projects will reinvigorate the central city
by attracting more people and businesses. Th e justice precinct alone will bring 2,000

Exclusive Economic Zone—Seismic Surveying
6. ANDREW WILLIAMS (NZ First)  to the Minister of Conservation : Has he
received any reports on the environmenta l impact of seismic surveying in the New
Zealand Exclusive Economic Zone?
23 Oct 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14185

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: My responsibilities as
Minister of Conservation rela te to the protection of mari ne mammals. I have received
reports on improving the management of the environmental impacts of seismic surveys.
The new law I introduced to Parliament as Minister for the Environment in August 2011
enables such effects to be regulated, whereas  prior to this when many seismic surveys
were done there were no rules. This has enabled the 2012 code of conduct for
minimising acoustic disturbance to marine ma mmals from seismic survey operations to
be introduced. I have received reports on updating and improvi ng it. It is just another
example of the improvements this Government is making to environmental law.

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: What environmental safeguards have been put in place in
relation to seismic surveying in the excl usive economic zone, and what monitoring
structure will be in place to provide comprehensive data and reporting on the
environmental impacts of seismic surveying?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I would be happy to provide the member the 2012 code of
conduct specifically about seismic survey ing, which also includes monitoring
requirements. I would point out that this code of conduct for seismic surveying has been
introduced only as a consequence of the law changes made by this Government and
opposed by members opposite, and that ma ny seismic surveys were done by the
previous Government with the support of New Zealand First with no standards at all.

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: What information does he have on any adverse effects on marine
wildlife as a result of seismic surveying?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The key issue for marine mammals in respect of seismic
surveying is the effects of the acoustic disturbance. That is where the Government has
done a huge amount of work. That is why that code of conduct was introduced last year.
That is why it is being updated this year, a nd that is why this Government has such a
proud record of improved environmental regulation.

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: Given the Minister’s answer and given New Zealand’s strong
international stance on protecting whales, dol phins, and other marine animals, will a
precautionary approach be taken to protect marine life if adverse effects of seismic
surveying are evident and proven?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The 2012 Code of Conduct fo r Minimising Acoustic
Disturbance to Marine Mammals from Seismic Survey Operations , including whales, is
world’s best practice around managing these risk s. It has become regulated only as a
consequence of this Government’s laws. I do have confidence that it enables us to be
able to utilise our re sources in the ocean environment while making sure we look after
those precious whales and dolphins.

Primary Growth Partnership—Successful Bids, Purpose, and Audit
8. IAN McKELVIE (National—Rangit īkei) to the Minister for Primary

items.speaker: Industries
items.text: What progress can he report on boosti ng innovation in the primary sector
through the Primary Growth Partnership?

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: The Primary Growth
Partnership has now committed $684 million of  industry and Government funds to 16
projects. Although these projects are long-term investments, they are already delivering
some very exciting outcomes. The Precision Seafood Harvesting project is developing a
new, world-leading net technol ogy. This high-tech equipmen t has the aim of allowing
fish to be sorted by size and species befo re even leaving the water. This has the
potential to revolutionise co mmercial fishing. Also, the New Zealand Sheep Industry
Transformation Project has already realised r eal gains. Its Silere meat premium brand
was introduced in 2012, and $45 million of branded products are in place. Also, Silere
was a winner amongst supporters of the America’s Cup just recently, where more than
1.4 tonnes of merino lamb was dished up during the 12 weeks.
23 Oct 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14187

items.speaker: Ian McKelvie
items.text: What other results are already bei ng realised in the Primary Growth
Partnership programmes?

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: A very good question. Transformi ng the Dairy Value Chain,
a Primary Growth Partnership programme, ha s already delivered some amazing results.
Last week Fonterra announced  a new $72 million investme nt into its Clandeboye
mozzarella plant near Timaru. This is driven by a new patented technology for
developing mozzarella cheese, which was supported by Primary Growth Partnership

dairy animal traits could re sult in an es timated 10 percent per year gain, worth $30

items.text: Why is the Government investi ng in innovation in the primary
sector?

Crime Victims—Support Services
10. PAUL FOSTER-BELL (National)  to the Minister of Police : What recent
announcements has she made to support the victims of serious financial crime?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Yesterday I announced that the Serious
Fraud Office has signed a memorandum of understanding with Victim Support. The
emotional and financial consequences for vi ctims of serious financial crime can be
extremely traumatic and, like other victims of serious crime, they deserve support. That
is why when I became the Minister I asked th e Serious Fraud Office to establish a close
working relationship with Victim Support. The resulting memorandum of understanding
will ensure that victims have access to help  and advice, as well as giving them the
confidence that those who commit financial fraud are held to account for their crimes.

items.speaker: Paul Foster-Bell
items.text: How will the memorandum of understanding result in better
services for victims of serious financial crime?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Serious financial crime can have a devastating impact on
victims, with many of them losing a lifetime of savings. The memorandum of
understanding will see the two agencies working together to promote and deliver victim
support services and to keep  victims informed about th eir cases. The Serious Fraud
Office and Victim Support will also hold joint training sessions to help share
information and best practice. The Seri ous Fraud Office has already published two
guides to help victims understand the proc esses involved in investigations and
prosecutions and how this might affect them.

Climate Change Policy—Emissions Trading Scheme
12. Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM (Green)  to the Minister for Climate Change

items.speaker: Issues
items.text: Will he explain, given the latest projection of New Zealand’s net greenhouse gas
emissions is around 90 million tonnes in 2040, how the Government can conceivably
reach its own emissions reduction target of 30 million tonnes by 2050?
Hon SIMON BRIDGES (Associate Mini ster for Climate Change Issues)  on
behalf of the Minister for Climate Change Issues : We will meet our targets through a
combination of the New Zealand emissions trading scheme and other domestic
initiatives. We will also likely use reduc tions from overseas where it makes good
economic sense to do so. The emissions trading scheme is a long-term tool, and it is not
hard to imagine that with a good outcome on a new global agreement and leadership
from the major economies, we wi ll need to adjust our own domestic policy response, as
well. We anticipate that the Ministry for th e Environment’s projections will continue to
change over the next 30 or 40 years.

items.speaker: Dr Kennedy Graham
items.text: But does he take responsibility for the fact that the latest
projections show that instead  of meeting a 50 percent redu ction in emissions, we are
heading for a 50 percent increase?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: No, because of course the projections are useful, but they
are also limited, given that they are based at the moment on a very low carbon price. We
know that as we make progress in internati onal negotiations, car bon price will surely
rise.

items.speaker: Dr Kennedy Graham
items.text: Can he then explain to this  House why New Zealand’s net
emissions have increased since 2009, the pe riod in which his Government has been
weakening the emissions trading scheme, with the result of a low carbon price?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: As I have just said, and it wa s implicit in my last answer,
it is a product at the moment of a low car bon price right around th e world. But what is
of course very true is that as we make progress internationally, it is highly likely that the
23 Oct 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14191
price will rise, and with that  the projections and the progress that we will make around
this world.

the Greens never—

failure on the part of this Government and its breach of our framework convention
obligations, other than the gutting of the em issions trading scheme over which he has

items.text: Why is the Care of Children Law Reform Bill required?

Bill): It is true that adoption numbers in New Ze aland are falling, but th is is in part due

Purpose
4. ANDREW LITTLE (Labour) to the Member in charge of the Privacy (Giving
Privacy Commissioner Necessary Tools) Amendment Bill : Why is the Privacy
(Giving Privacy Commissioner Necessary Tools) Amendment Bill required?
SUE MORONEY (Member in charge of the Privacy (Giving Privacy
Commissioner Necessary Tools) Amendment Bill) : This bill gives two important
tools to the Privacy Commissioner: firstly, th e ability to launch he r own investigation,
without a specific complaint, in order to investigate a privacy breach; and, secondly, the
right to require agencies to take specific remedies when there are privacy problems.
Both of these issues, which are in this bill, were recommended by the Law Commission.

items.text: Why is it important to New Zealanders for this bill to be progressed
now?

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: It is important that this bill is progressed now because of this
Government’s record of playing fast and loose with New Zealanders’ privacy—
breaches everywhere from ACC to the Earthquake Commission—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That answer is quite sufficient.

23 Oct 2013 General Debate 14193

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: I move, That the House take note of
miscellaneous business. As if the Skycity deal was not  rotten enough—as if it was not
rotten enough—we now have one of the most unethical bills ever to pass through this
House’s history sneaked through on the votes  of not one but two deeply conflicted
Government MPs. When the Opposition is dow n one member due to the by-election, it
is an abuse of democracy to pass the New Zealand International Convention Centre Bill
in such circumstances.
MPs are under huge pressure to  vote against this deal. Th e pressure is coming from
families, churches, and organisations that have been harmed by problem gambling or
left to mop up its mess. Sam Lotu-Iiga knows all about this pressu re. He represents a
community guided by deeply he ld religious beliefs that is genuinely troubled by
gambling. How convenient, then, that a suppos ed spokesperson for the Catholic Church
should front up to a select committee with evidence that the Church thinks that the
casino is really a pretty good place—in fact, a safer place to  gamble. But that was not
the Church’s view of the cas ino at all. The Church does not support this deal. The man
who gave that evidence was none other than Sam Lotu-Iiga ’s own electorate chairman,
Seamus Donegan. When Mr Donegan gave the evidence, Sam Lotu-Iiga sat listening in
silence. He never once revealed his relati onship with the man, not even in the days
afterwards, when the Church had to distan ce itself from Mr Donegan’s comments and
set the public record straight. I say that Mr Lotu-Iiga’s silen ce over all these weeks
speaks volumes. My only hope is that he is troubled enough by his conscience to allow
it to be heard when the time comes to vote for this unethical, morally compromised bill.
John Banks is also deeply conflicted ove r this bill. John Banks has railed like a
preacher against the evils of gambling in th e past. He has called casino operators “wide
boys”. He has accused them of having “s ucked, hung, drawn, [and ] quartered,” the
people of New Zealand. But just $15,000 late r, he has changed his tune. Asked by
reporters how he could in al l honesty support the deal, John Banks replied that he did
not gamble and he did not drink, but he did not inflict his values on others. Well, then,
why did he vote to raise the drinking age to 20? Of course he inflicts his values on
others. He just disappears from his values when it suits him.
John Banks is a textbook case of conflict. When a member votes on a deal worth
$400 million to a casino while at the same time the casino’s chief executive officer is in
court giving evidence against him, there is a conflict of interest. It is a conflict of
interest burden that is borne by Mr Banks. Th e rules around conflicts of interest exist in
this Parliament for a reason. Even the per ception of a conflict is  enough to require
standard management: declaration of the c onflict and, in some ca ses, removing oneself
from the decision making. It happens all the time and is the best way to manage the
conflict or perceived conflict. The Skycity bi ll deserves to go down in a ball of flames
as the perfect example of the Key Government’s crony capitalist values.
Regardless of the bill, the Green Party has produced  proposals for making New
Zealanders safer from problem gambling anyway. We will make  pre-commitment on
pokies compulsory, rather than voluntary, so gamblers will have to set a limit at the
outset and will not be able to exceed it in the heat of the moment. This is effective in the
same way that compulsory seatbelts are e ffective, whereas volunt ary seatbelts are not.
We will outlaw inducements by casinos to pr oblem gamblers to encourage them to
come back to gamble. We know that that happens because 67 percent of the pokie
revenue at Skycity Casino comes from gamblers who are part of the loyalty programme.
So it knows who they are, it knows where they live, it knows that that programme is
supposed to be used to prevent harm, and yet that is used by Skycity  to market to those
14194 General Debate 23 Oct 2013
problem gamblers. We will stop that across th e board, including for Skycity. Yes, these
ideas come about through our fight over the S kycity deal, but they exist on their own as
reasonable, practical, and responsible ways to stop problem gambling. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: The member who has just
resumed her seat, Metiria Turei, tried to im ply that members in this House feel under
some pressure to vote for the Skycity c onvention centre bill. We ll, I can tell you, the
only pressure the members in this party feel under is to turn round 9 years of complete
economic sabotage and destruction that was wreaked on this country by a Labour-Green
Government. The pressure I feel as a member of this House is the pressure to provide
opportunities and jobs for New Zealanders. I w ould be surprised if there was anyone in
this House who would stand up and tell New Zealand that they come here every day and
block every single opportunity to create jobs in New Zeal and. Yet what do we have?
We have some parties who come to this House and they oppose agriculture, they oppose
free trade, they oppose the roll-out of ultra- fast broadband and all the benefits that
brings, they oppose mining, they oppose every opportunity that would create jobs, and
they support every bureaucratic, process-h eavy, costly, long, drawn-out process that
will suck the life out of the economic future of New Zealand.
I want to talk a littl e bit about one issue th at we are hearing a lo t about just recently,
and that is the issue of mineral explorati on. I want to talk about mineral exploration
because I find it absolutely unbelievable that we have parties in this House with the
barefaced cheek to come in here and talk about the risks of oil and gas drilling, when
they not only spent 9 years in Government  with zero protection for the environment—
zero protection for the environment—and zero rules around how we look after our
offshore resources when we do these things  but also voted against environmental
protection when the National Government put it up. It was the National Government
that, for the first time, instituted a system of environmental consenting for our offshore
exclusive economic zone and continental shelf. And do you know what happened, of
course? Labour voted against it and the Greens voted against it.
What I want to do is tell you a little bit abou t what the proce ss was under a Labour-
Green Government. This was the environm ental protection. This was the very
technically competent, incl usive, publicly involved process under Labour and that the

items.speaker: Greens had. Step one
items.text: the Minister of Energy and Resources signs a permit. That is it.
That was the whole of the process. So wh ere was the environmental protection? Where
was Greenpeace with its models? Wh ere was the public involvement? [ Interruption]
And now we see the outrage—the outrage—that pours off them in waves.
But do you know what I think it is? I think we can take a little bit of a lesson on this
from what is happening now with the Skyc ity bill. We have got Labour saying publicly
“What an outrage!” and saying privately “Don’t worry, boys. We ’ll look after you.
We’ll be fine if it’s in.” So you can imag ine what Labour is te lling the oil and gas
industry behind the scenes: “Don’t worry, we’ll be out there, charging about saying how
outrageous it is, but we’ll see you right. Don’t worry.” Y ou could not figure out what
the Labour position was on this issue if you tried. You know that whatever the members
tell you is unlikely to be co rrect. We have had David Cun liffe telling Taranaki that
people are leaving in droves, and yet what were the numbers that came out? No, it was
growth in Taranaki.

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: In fact, with a successful blend of oil and gas, agriculture, and
tourism—Mr Jonathan Young will know—it is one of the most successful economies in
the country.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Where are the jobs?
23 Oct 2013 General Debate 14195

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: The jobs, Mr Clark, come from mineral extraction. They come
from agriculture. They come from the roll-out of infrastructure like the ultra-fast
broadband network. If New Z ealand is not already wise  enough to know how much
damage the Labour-Green Government did in its 9 years, the fact that those members
oppose more jobs in agricultu re, oppose more jobs in th e oil and gas sector, oppose
more jobs across the provinces, and oppose th e roll-out of infrastructure—you do have
to wonder. But I can tell them. Perhaps I ca n help them. Perhaps we can help the Green
Party cut out some hundreds of thousands of do llars with its spin doctors that, frankly,
the oil and gas sector, through its taxes, proba bly paid for. We can tell it already what
its slogan should be in 2014:  “The Green Party. We’re for New Zealand—closed for
business. Last man out, blow out the candle.”

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: If the member Amy Adams wants to talk about
jobs, then we can talk about jobs. Let us be  absolutely clear. Th is election will be won
and lost on the economy and jobs. This Governme nt’s failure is to act in the face of
massive job losses in this country. All that the Government members are interested in
doing is preserving their relationships th rough dodgy deals with organisations like
Skycity.
One such example, which I raised in this H ouse yesterday, is the crisis that is going
on in the screen industry in New Zealand. I do not use the word “crisis” lightly, but that
is absolutely what we are facing. There are literally hundreds, up to thousands, of jobs
and livelihoods being lost as we speak. The crime of it all is that it is entirely
preventable, but this out-of-touch Governme nt is sitting on the sidelines while this
absolutely critical industry is decimated. Of course, we have ha d this industry for a
number of years. But in 2004, when the in centives regime came in under the then
Labour Government, it undeniably gave a boos t to the industry. The industry met the
new demand. It built up skills. It built up talent. It built up capital. Now we have got to a
point where if a production comes into New Zealand, we can meet the needs of that
production, with up to 90 percen t internally in New Zealan d, with the sk ill base and
with the capital that we have.
But since then, things have changed drama tically. We have the people, but the work
is disappearing and it is disa ppearing fast. Why? Well, first of all, undeniably the Kiwi
dollar is high and it is having an impact. Since the incentive regime has come in, the
Kiwi dollar has gone up in strength against th e American dollar by 25 percent. That has
virtually decimated the drawcard that our re bate regime once was.  The fact that our
regime has remained static while other countries—

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: “Moaning Myrtle”—what’s the answer?

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: —have become more competitive has meant that we are in an
entirely preventable perfect storm. And ther e are answers, Tau Henare. There are things
that this Government could be doing. Labour  has said that the Government should be
intervening on monetary policy. That is what  we would do. If it is unwilling to act in
that regard, if it is unwilling to do that, th en it should at least look at the relative
competitiveness of the rebate regime—and it is a rebate. Essentially, it is money in
before money goes out. You have to pay taxes and you have to have economic spin-offs
before anything happens in that regard.
Why is the Government not doi ng anything? Well, firstly, it claims that the rebate at
the moment is somehow at a break-even poi nt. Well, I ask one question. The Ministry
of Business, Innovation and Em ployment should go and look at  why the UK, Australia,
Hungary, Ireland, the USA, and Canada are doi ng things differently. That is one simple
question I ask of those members. Secondly, th e Government claims that our skills base
will naturally attract people, but our skills are just one part of  the mix. If the rest of the
mix does not attract production, it does not  matter whether we have good people here.
14196 General Debate 23 Oct 2013
In fact, the Government tried to argue that one of the reasons that the rebate regime was
cost-neutral was that if all those skilled people did not have work in screen production,
they would just go somewhere else.
I have met good people, talented people at the top of their game, who have been
unemployed for months. They will leave this  country, leave these shores, and we will
not have the talent base for those production companies when they come back into this
country. The fact the Government does not acknowledge that shows that it is completely
out of touch and does not understand this industr y. It is not just tale nt; it is capital. I
challenge Steven Joyce to go and visit the co mpanies that invested  in the rigging, the
kit, and the props. Those props are going to landfills because the companies cannot
afford to store them any more. It is kit th at they can no longer afford to keep and are
selling off. It is not just about the big projects . The big projects prop up the little
projects, the New Zealand projects that help us tell stories about ourselves.
This Government is standing on the sideline s while an important, skilled industry is
being decimated and jobs are being lost. Let that be on those members’ heads if they
continue to stand on the sidelines and do nothing while we lose this critical industry.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: That speech from
Jacinda Ardern was almost as angry as my  little speech on John Campbell’s show last
week. But I will tell you this much—at least Jacinda Ardern and I did not give a nasty
little speech like Metiria Turei did in the House not long ago.
Speaking of John Campbell, Greenpeace, Gareth Hughes, and Moana Mackey have
all been very excited in the last few days about oil and gas, and there is a lot to be
excited about with oil and gas. We in this country have a pr oud history in this area. We
have a great presence today, and we have a very strong future. Today the average wage
in oil and gas mining is $105,000—what is not to like? That is over double the New
Zealand average. Actually, if you take just j obs in petroleum, it is probably more than
that, if you get rid of other mining on the side. They are very high-paying jobs—the
highest in this country. The people working in that industry are the kind whom members
on the other side of this House say they  represent but actually do not—they do not.
Those workers have come to our side of this House because they know that we are the
ones delivering the future for them.
I said we have got a proud history in this ar ea. It is actually on our coat of arms. We
have had an extractive econom y for a very long time, since Moturoa in 1865. Actually,
as I understand it, that was the second oil rig in the world, af ter one that I think was in
Pennsylvania. So we have been doing this for a very long time. Since the 1960s over
1,000 wells have been drilled safely in Ne w Zealand without a major incident—200
offshore, and eight deep offshore, in over 300 metres. So we have a very proud history
in this area.
Today there are numbers that are not to be sniffed at by the Greens. I am talking
about $2.5 billion to $3 billion per annum, and $800 million in royalt ies, which pay for
the schools, the hospitals, and the other infrastructure that everyone in this House agrees
with. Our fourth-highest commodity is crude oil to Australia. It is our biggest export. It
is literally an industry that feeds and clothe s children in this country. It delivers taxes
and royalties, and, as I have said, in te rms of the dollars going into households, it
delivers more than anything else.
Then we talk about the future, and what a great future it is. We should be excited
about the biggest exploration season ever , probably, on most measures, this coming
season and about what that means for this c ountry down the track in  terms of jobs. The
truth is that we are under-e xplored. We have one basin, Taranaki, that gives us $2.5
billion or thereabouts in  revenue. One more, as I have sa id before in this House, would
23 Oct 2013 General Debate 14197
be a game changer for this country. It would mean more people employed in high-
income jobs.
I think Statistics New Zealand said that 130,000 M āori are working in Australia,
thousands of them in oil and gas mining. Well, let me tell you that they would like to
work in this country if they had the opportun ity, and that is what this Government is
about. It is about real jobs for the real pe ople whom the left lik es to talk about—but
whom we are actually doing something for. And what a great speech that was from
Amy Adams, where we heard about the enviro nmental protections that we have put in
place. It was a very layered set of protections  that mean that up front we are preventing
the kinds of harms that the scaremongers in the Greens like to go on about.
You know, it is interesting to see from the le ft a very schizophrenic approach to this,
an approach that is all ove r the show. I agree with Shane Jones that the Greenpeace
report today was “greenwash”. Actually, I th ink I almost agree w ith David Shearer. He
seems to be moderating his position. He says  that provided that we have world’s best
standards—which we do, and which we have  implemented through the Crown minerals
regime this year—then that is OK. See—he is  shaking his head, so he does not support
it. He has gone back, so he is schizophrenic. He has gone back into the Moana Mackey -
Maryan Street camp. He does not know where he is.
At least with the Greens, we know their position. They are totally opposed to
progress in this country. What they do not unde rstand is that it is not a zero-sum game.
It is not an either/or. Actually, we can be proud that we have 75 percent renewables in
this country—the third-highest in the world and going up—but not if Labour and the
Greens get their way with the disincentive there will be for investment in renewables
going forward.
DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First) : It will not be long befo re it is 3 years since the
February 2011 Christchurch earthquake. It is now over 3 years since the September
2010 Greendale fault earthquake. Who would have thought that after that period of time
there would still be people trying to settle  insurance claims, let alone actually getting
progress on the rebuilding of their homes?
Let it be recorded for posterity that the constant delays by in surers over Canterbury
earthquake claims, the failures by insurers to honour their policies, the treatment by
insurers of the people who placed their trust in their policies and those companies, and
the full replacement insurance that has not actua lly meant what it sa id have all defined
what is one of the most disgraceful epis odes in New Zealand’s commercial history.
Never has such utterly despicable behaviour been seen by commercial insurers on such
a scale in this country. We are not talking about just a few cases; we are not talking
about just a small minority of difficult cases,  but literally hundreds of cases—in fact, a
very significant percentage of the whole. It is a national disgrace that this should still be
the case 3 years from the disaster. We are not  talking about just a few of the insurers,
but all of them—some are better than others.
The current situation is truly an indictment on the insurance industry in New Zealand
as a whole. Among the worst is an entity  known as Southern Response Earthquake
Services. Is that not a great name? Well, it would be, if it were true. But “response” is
exactly what it is not. This is the entity that took over a fa iled insurer, AMI Insurance.
AMI was so inept that when the first major disaster came along, for which it was
required to be prepared, it did not last 5 minutes and had to be taken over by the
Government.
That should have solved the problem, should it not? Well, no, it did not. Anyone who
saw the Campbell Live show recently would know for sure that Southern Response is
just another one of the shonky insurers that we are all so disgusted with in Christchurch.
It is just another failure. It  is just another incompetent pe rformer. It is just another
14198 General Debate 23 Oct 2013
delayer. It is just another arrogant a nd unhelpful obstacle for policyholders. In the
meantime, people suffer. Health suffers, families suffer, and communities suffer.
Christchurch people have had enough of it.  What on earth has the Government been
doing about it? The Government was told years a go that it needed to intervene, just as
the Australian Government intervened in past  disasters there. That Government did not
tolerate the incompetence of insurers; it legislated, it regulated, and it made sure that its
people were not put through what ours have been put through.
After the first 2 years, all this National Government would do is provide some free
advisers, not even advocates. The response from our Government since has been a long,
deafening silence. So after th e next election, when New Zeal and First forms part of the
next Government, it will seek to establish a new State insurance company to replace the
one sold by Labour. We will get a new one—“ KiwiSure”—to ensure that there is a
reliable insurer that will give genuine repl acement insurance and deal with disaster
claims promptly and fairly. That is why th is country needs New Z ealand First, because
it needs good governance and people need a fair go.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Kia
ora tātou. Mr O’Rourke talked about a lot of suffering. The four bills that came before
this House this morning followed pretty much the same theme. We have been
fortunate—or unfortunate—today to have traversed a lot of  history for the people of
Tūhoe, Ng āti Hau ā, Ng āti Koroki Kahukura, and, of c ourse, the descendants of
Mokomoko. Their legacies are relived; their experiences arrived he re in Parliament
today. It is in the spirit of that sort of sorro w that I wanted to focus this contribution this
afternoon, on our tamariki and our mokopuna and, indeed, the mokopuna of Tūhoe.
In this morning’s paper, under the headin g “Child abuse is rising in NZ”, the
Children’s Commissioner, Russell Wills, re vealed that the public’s tolerance for
violence against children stil l had a way to go. I got asked the question of how we as a
nation can hold our heads high when our child abuse statistics are such an indictment on
our reputation. Our focus as members of Par liament should rightly and properly be on
what we are doing as agents of the State. As  such, I would implore all members of this
House to read the statement released just 3 days ago on Marae Investigates by a leading
paediatric specialist, Professo r Innes Asher. I referred to th at in a speech this morning.
Professor Asher—a clinician at the Starship hospital, a paediatric ian for over 30 years,
and the head of the paediatrics department  at Auckland University—has spent her life
investing in the well-being of children. So wh en she described the treatment of children
during the Tūhoe raids 6 years ago as “one of the worst cases of child abuse by the State
in recent years”, one would think that this House would listen.
Of course, it is not the first time that the children of Ru ātoki have been raised in
public attention. A mere 5 months ago a re port from the Independent Police Conduct
Authority recommended that changes to polic y and practice needed to be introduced
that would reflect better pl anning for children and vulnerable people. Aside from that, I
am still waiting for the Human Rights Comm ission report to come out, and hopefully
that will be soon.
At the time of this recent release the local schoolteacher Gaylene Collier reflected
that her pupils had alre ady been frightened when they were detained in their homes
during the operation. Her conclusions were pr etty clear: “It was tough on the families
and it should never ever have happened.” I ha ve relentlessly brought the issues of these
families to this House, but we are still a fa r way away from seeing any resolution to the
lasting trauma that Professo r Asher speaks of. On public te levision on Sunday she told
New Zealand that “if these children had been held by armed offenders in the same way,
the state would have immediately rescued those children and given them some help and
assistance. And the children would have been on the front page of the papers and on
23 Oct 2013 General Debate 14199
your lead news item,”. So why is it that we cannot face up to the wrongs done to the
innocent children caught up in Operation Eight ? Why are we so reluctant to admit that
the events of that day repres ent, as Professor Asher stat es, the most profound abuse of
power in our memory?
In a letter written to former Commissioner of Police Howard Broad, Peter Williams
QC described the extent of the terror raids as being “a great show of force by the police
who have been accompanied by military-type vehicles, helicopters, fire arms, dogs, and
various other adjuncts. Most of these police officers were dressed in military battle
uniform, consisting of black clothing, balacl avas, and carrying what appears to be
loaded weapons—in particular, rifles and revol vers.” One of the interviewees said that
he counted 43 police officers surrounding the ho use where he lived with his partner, his
four young children, his father, and his father’s  partner. All of these police had guns
trained on this house. These prisoners, ma inly women and children, were kept under
armed guard and detained for varying periods between 3 and 6 hours. The children,
particularly, were terrified, he said.
I do not understand how we can receive that sort of information and how we can hear
the horrific experiences our State forced upon children and not feel motivated to change
or to act. We could go to the Ruātoki valley. We could sit with the people of Tūhoe. We
could share with the wh ānau our acknowledgment of wh at happened on 15 October
2007 and that it had truly trauma tic effects on the chil dren that will affect them for the
rest of their lives. Our job as a Parliament is to represent the best interests of our people.
This is beyond party politics. It is beyond bureaucracy. This is about our children.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: Well, I would have thought  that the Minister of
Labour, Simon Bridges, may have had a word to say about the fact that it is Labour
weekend this weekend. However—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: No, he didn’t say it at all.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: —he did not say a word about Labour Day being this weekend.
He will just be off having a holiday, forget ting that Labour Day is about remembering
the struggle we had that began in 1840 for an  8-hour working day and forgetting that it
has been celebrated in this country from 1900.
There was a time when each generation was proud to say that their kids would be
better off at work than they were. We have all worked hard to ensure the rights won by
our forebears have not been lost. But I cannot say that to day. Working people are going
backwards under this National-led Governme nt. Our kids cannot get jobs, and even
when they do they are highly precarious. Fl exibility is about how easily they can be
fired and how little responsibility an em ployer must bear. Competitiveness and
productivity is about how low the wages can be and how much can be extracted from
workers in an ever-diminishing pool of hours. The 8-hour day and 40-hour week are
considered a joke. In fact they do not exist in legislation, and we have no working hours
protection in New Zealand.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Especially not in the forestry industry.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: Especially not in the forestry industry. We subsidise low
wages through Working for Families. We pay employers to take on young minimum-
wage workers, whom they can sack after 90 days. Then we blame people when they
struggle to make ends meet.
There are more and more people out looking for work now, for jobs that do not exist.
When they cannot find them they get punish ed. We are on a punishment regime led by
the Hon Paula Bennett.
Thousands of workers continue to lose th eir jobs through lay-offs. It has been a
dreadful week this week. I want to just  briefly send aroha out to the 1,000-odd New
Zealand Post workers who are facing the job losses that have been announced today.
14200 General Debate 23 Oct 2013
But what does this Government do? It goe s back to its normal modus operandi of
cutting workers’ rights. I guess that Simon Bridges should have been at the select
committee to hear the stories of workers,  the 14,000 workers who submitted against his
Employment Relations Amendment Bill. Howe ver, because he was not there, I am
going to tell some of their stories.
There is no story stronger th an that of the cleaners who wo rk in this Parliament, who
have appealed to Simon Bridges to not make their lives worse by ditching the
protections of Part 6A  of the Employment Relations Ac t. I hope he has been listening
like he said he would, and like he told this Parliament he would, but just in case here are
some words from the cleaners: “You never see us. Every evening we catch the bus or
the train from Wainuiomata or Porirua to clean your office. We vacuum the floors,
scrub the toilets and tidy away your rubbish. We come in at midnight when you have all
gone home, and the Parliament Buildings are empty.”

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: Where are all the Pacific Island union organisers?

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: I know Tau Henare is a bit se nsitive about this topic. “We
come over to Parliament after we have wo rked all night cleaning the buildings on The
Terrace and Lambton Quay. It’s a hard j ob, a dirty job, but we don’t mind being
cleaners. We are proud to clean the most im portant house in the country. But we don’t
love our pay ... On top of that as contracted workers, we f ace daily uncertainty at work.
Spotless has the contract to clean Parliament but it could lose it so do not make it bad
for cleaners or make it worse for cleaners, Mr Bridges. Part 6A is a fair rule. All the
contractors should play by the same rules.” On their behalf  I call on Simon Bridges to
remove the changes he is planning to make to Part 6A.
In Christchurch he should have heard th e stories too from wo rkers who came along,
who have already been traumatised by the earthquake, who said: “Why would a
Government want to cut our pay? Why would they do that to us?” There was a worker
called Julie Reason, who talked about he r job as a home-care worker—a home-care
worker working on assignment, job to job, wo rking an hour then ge tting in the car,
getting paid nothing, no tea breaks or anything. She said: “Why would this Government
want to cut our pay?”
My message to New Zealand workers this  Labour Day is that the Labour Party
values the hard work of working New Zealanders and their contribution. We are on your
side, and we have real plan s to improve your working lives when this Government is
thrown out.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: Well, today on the front page
of the Taranaki Daily News we saw Greenpeace’s estimation of the oil reserves off the
North Taranaki coast—40,000 barrels a day. That is double the rate of flow of the Maari
field, which is offshore from South Taranaki.
I have got to say that Greenpeace’s modelling is the best advertising I have seen of
New Zealand’s prospectivity. That should get the attention of oil explorers all over the
world. We are the new Mozambique, or the Texas or the Norway of the south. The
royalties and tax revenues coming from these fields will make New Zealand one of the
wealthiest countries in the southern hemisphe re. There will be schoo ls, hospitals, roads,
operations, and continual New Zealand superannuation for 65-year-olds.
I want to look at th e example of Norway and what it has done with the significant
reserves it has been able to extract. Norway is so similar to New Zealand in many ways.
It is the second-least densel y populated country in Europe. It is a very long country—
1,600 kilometres long. We are ju st a little bit longer, at 2,000 kilometres. The capital
city Oslo is the largest in the nation, w ith a population of nearly 1 million people.
Auckland, of course, has an urban population of 1.4 million people.
23 Oct 2013 General Debate 14201
What has Norway done with its extensive reserves of petroleum, natural gas and
minerals, lumber, seafood, fresh water, and hydropower? That count ry has the fourth-
highest per capita income in the world. That is good news. On a per capita basis it is the
world’s largest producer of oil and natural gas outside th e Middle East. Listen to this:
“The country maintains a welfare model with universal health care, subsidised higher
education, and a comprehensive social security  system.” Why do they have such social
advantages in Norway? Simply because of petroleum production. The OECD ranks
Norway third in social mobility and fourth in its 2013 Better Life index. Forbes ranks
Norway fourth in its list of the world’s ri chest countries, which compares countries by
GDP.

items.speaker: This is the bizarre thing
items.text: all these so cial improvements in Norway have come
through its oil and gas production. These are the same social improvements that the
Green Party advocates for, except the Green Pa rty does not want to pay for it. It does
not want to see the source of this social ch ange and social uplift being the work and the
generation of an industry in oil and gas.
The Green Party, along with it s red friends, says no to ju st about everything. Unless,
of course, you are David Cunliffe—then you say no to the TV cameras and yes to big
business behind the public’s back. Do you doubt that? Not one little bit. David Cunliffe
promised the world to his union supporters at the Coun cil of Trade Unions. He
promised a living wage and extended parent al leave, but then he backtracked when
talking to the media immedi ately afterwards, saying “We don’t know when.” and “We
need to be fiscally responsible.” Labour members get all angsty about oil exploration on
the East Coast, but turn up in droves in Ta ranaki, licking the boot s of the oil barons.
That is what they do.
Labour is a two-faced party wi th no clear and distinct policy. Its members are still
divided and still incoherent. They have shallow one-liners, but no depth and consistency
in their policy. This is not the time—in fact, it is never the time—for that sort of
fractured group to be anywhere near the Treasury benches.
Do we want the same progress, wealth, and social infrastructure that Norway has?
Yes, indeed. Taranaki stands out as an exam ple of that. Statistics New Zealand released
the first official analysis of regional gr oss domestic product. That study covers the
period from 2007 to 2010, and on a regional ba sis Taranaki recorded the highest growth
in GDP due to the expansion of its oil and gas industry during this period. Taranaki’s
economy increased by 46.9 percent in size over th e 4 years, the largest increase of any
region, due to expansion in oil and gas production. The region boasts the highest GDP
per person, beyond any other region in the country. Taranaki’s strength—just as I
close—in mining and agriculture gave us the highest gross domestic product per person
of $73,200 against a national average of $43,700. That is 67 percent higher. Thank you.

items.speaker: CAROL BEAUMONT
items.text: Well, I want to follow my colleague Darien
Fenton and talk about what is happening to women in the paid workforce. Certainly,
women are going backwards under this National Government. Women are not
experiencing the brighter future that National promised. National’s rich corporate mates,
on the other hand, of course, are getting lots of attention and lots  of opportunities, but
not women seeking to get ahead financially —not women trying to manage paid and
unpaid work responsibilities.
As others have noted, the job situation is dire, unemployment remains high, and yet
National promised 170,000 new jobs over 4 y ears in 2011, and in 2012 managed to
muster just 8,000.
Of course, over recent days we have seen workers losing their jobs from a
fellmongery in Shannon, New Zealand Post work ers are hearing today that they will be
losing their jobs, and the mill workers in Ro torua heard on Monday that they will be
14202 General Debate 23 Oct 2013
losing their jobs—many, many workers. I want  to convey my concern to those workers
and I know just how difficult that will be.
It is not only unemployment that is a problem, though; underemployment also
remains a problem. Over 100,000 people want more work. I am sure that the majority of
those workers would be women seeking more  hours than they currently have. Women
are low paid. Women are overrepresented am ongst those in low-pa id work—certainly,
at least 60 percent of those on the minimum wage. Of course, the Government fails to
make any meaningful shift in  the minimum wage, and fails to commit to a living wage.
And who does that affect? Who does that aff ect? Well, of course it affects those women
workers, but it also affects their families. It has an impact on their lifetime earnings. It
means that with an ageing population wher e women tend to live longer, women are
more likely to be living in poverty in their old age.
What is the Government’s response to low pay? Well, John Key thinks it is a great
idea, actually. He is quoted as saying that  driving wages down is a good thing. In the
Employment Relations Act changes, the attacks on workers’ rights will make the
situation worse by undermining collective bargaining. Certainly, the Committee on the
Elimination of Discrimination against Women, the international UN committee
concerned about women, has said  that we need to look at the gendered impact of this
legislation. What has the Government said? “No action to be taken.”
What about pay equity? This is not someth ing that the Government is committed to.
The Government says that greater economic independence for women is meant to be a
priority, but it says that will be done by m oving women out of low-paid work, rather
than by valuing and paying for that work. We ll, who is going to do the work in aged
care, for example? When are we going to see th at properly valued? There is barely any
mention of pay equity on the Ministry of  Women’s Affairs website. Certainly, the
Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women again refers to that,
and, again, there is no action to be taken.
Recently, a very brave women, Kristine Bart lett, won a case against her employer,
TerraNova Homes and Care, an aged-care employer. She earns $14.46 an hour after 20
years’ service in aged care. What is the Government saying? Well, the Minister of
Women’s Affairs is not interested. She has not briefed the Minister of Labour. She has
not even had a conversation with the Minister  of Labour about this important issue. The
Minister of Labour, when questioned in the House, just makes jokes. So, clearly, pay
equity is not something that the Government is concerned about.
Paid parental leave would help families manage their income when they have a new
child. Of course, my colleague here, Sue Mo roney, is actively promoting an extension
to 26 weeks. There is massive community s upport for it and it has a majority in this
House, but, no, the Government intends to veto that change.
I want to talk particularly about indus try training because industry training is
supposedly how women might move into these non-traditional jobs, and yet the
